I have seen R, and Python recommending as good "entry" levels for general, scientific computing, that are relatively "easy" to understand. Especially with a "bioinformatics" bent. hell, this was just a quick google search away.

The problem is that with most programming languages, it really is application dependent, and the tools that are available at your institution. Bioinformatics, like genetic sequencing is one thing, actually coding electronics/imaging/signal analysis for monitoring is another.

Honestly, your best bet would be to talk to own of your TAs, or one of your professors, after researching some of their projects on their profile page, which should be linked through their department, as well as some of their published papers. By the sounds of it, you still have some electives in the future, you can look at course syllabus of past offerings, and get an understanding of what is expected. You can literally bring up the fact you are looking to improve your skills, so that you are better equipped to tackle certain topics later, and you can get first hand advice from the people who will help shape your final projects/reports in whatever specialty you look to get into.
